def: A unit of power equal to one million watts. A 100 MW data center draws as much electricity as approximately 80,000 average U.S. homes.
Electrical infrastructure that steps down high-voltage transmission power to usable levels. Large data centers require dedicated substations, often funded by ratepayers.
A cooling method that uses water evaporation to remove heat. Highly water-intensive — a large facility may consume 1–5 million gallons per day.

Payment in Lieu of Taxes. A negotiated arrangement where a developer pays a reduced, fixed amount instead of standard property taxes — often locking in decades of reduced revenue for schools and services.

A zoning classification that permits a use without requiring a public hearing or discretionary approval. Data centers are often permitted by-right in industrial zones, removing the public's chance to weigh in.
A ratio measuring how efficiently a data center uses energy. A PUE of 1.0 is perfect; industry average is 1.5–1.6, meaning 50–60% overhead energy beyond computing.
A tradeable certificate representing one MWh of renewable electricity generation. Purchasing RECs does not mean a facility runs on renewable power — it offsets on paper only.
Data centers exceeding 100 MW and typically 100,000+ square feet, operated by or for major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google, Meta, etc.).
